solution.concept_anchor: Federal Part of 1935 Act never implemented
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students who know the Act introduced a federal structure assume it was operationalized, unaware that only the provincial portions came into force in 1937.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options claiming the entire 1935 Act was implemented in 1937 — only Part II (provincial autonomy) came into force that year.

Eliminate options suggesting the federation failed because princes were unwilling to negotiate — the specific legal threshold (52 of 104 Chamber of Princes seats + half of total princely state population) was never met.
Identify the option that correctly states the Federal Part was never operationalized while the Provincial Part was — this is option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with the 1935 Act commonly recall that it introduced a federal structure and assume this federal arrangement was implemented alongside provincial autonomy in 1937. The trap lies in conflating the architecture of the Act with its actual implementation. The Federal Part of the Act required princely states to accede voluntarily through an Instrument of Accession, and the threshold of 52 of 104 Chamber of Princes seats plus states representing half the total princely population was never achieved. As a result, the All-India Federation never came into existence, and the Central Legislature under the 1919 Act continued to function.
solution.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1935 is often studied as a monolithic reform, but its two core parts had very different fates. The Provincial Part (Part II), introducing provincial autonomy, was operationalized on April 1, 1937. The Federal Part, envisaging an All-India Federation of British Indian provinces and princely states, was never implemented.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 1935 Act was not implemented in its entirety in 1937. Only the provincial provisions came into force.
• Option (b) — Correct: Only the Provincial Part was operationalized in 1937; the Federal Part lapsed entirely because the requisite number of princely states never acceded.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The federation did not fail due to Congress opposition alone; the legal threshold for princely state accession was the primary obstacle.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The federation was not replaced by a transitional arrangement — it simply never came into existence.

Value Addition:
• The threshold required 52 of 104 Chamber of Princes seats and states with half of total princely population to accede.
• The Central Legislature under the Government of India Act 1919 continued to function at the Centre until 1947.
• The concept of voluntary accession via Instrument of Accession resurfaced in 1947 for post-independence integration of princely states.

solution.concept_anchor: Residuary powers vested in Governor-General not Parliament

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1935 divided legislative subjects into three lists — Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent — a structure that directly preceded the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act introduced the tripartite division with 59 Federal, 54 Provincial, and 36 Concurrent subjects, which served as the template for the three lists in the Seventh Schedule of the 1950 Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 1935 Act, residuary powers of legislation were vested in the Federal Legislature, paralleling the position under the Indian Constitution where residuary powers rest with Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the 1935 Act, residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General, not the Federal Legislature. Under the Indian Constitution, residuary powers vest with Parliament (Union), not with the President.

statement_analysis.statement: In the event of a conflict between federal and provincial legislation on a Concurrent List subject, the federal legislation was to prevail under the 1935 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The supremacy of Federal Legislature over concurrent subjects was established in the 1935 Act, mirroring Article 254 of the Indian Constitution which gives Parliament's law precedence over state laws on concurrent subjects.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because statements 1 and 3 are correct and students who partially recall the residuary powers provision may assume it too matches the Indian Constitution, making all three seem correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2 carefully — residuary powers under the 1935 Act went to the Governor-General, NOT to the Federal Legislature, making Statement 2 incorrect.
Confirm Statement 1 — the three-list structure with those subject counts is well established as the precursor to the Seventh Schedule, so Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 3 — federal supremacy on Concurrent List subjects was a feature of the 1935 Act, so Statement 3 is correct.
With Statements 1 and 3 correct and Statement 2 incorrect, the answer is option c (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is a classic entity-swap: students know residuary powers go to the Union/Parliament under the Indian Constitution and assume the same logic applied under the 1935 Act. In reality, the 1935 Act vested residuary powers in the Governor-General — an executive authority — not any legislature. This contrast is precisely what makes this a favourite UPSC comparison point between the 1935 Act and the 1950 Constitution.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act's legislative division is one of its most structurally significant features and a key precursor to the Indian Constitution's Seventh Schedule.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The three-list structure (59 Federal, 54 Provincial, 36 Concurrent subjects) was the direct forerunner of the Seventh Schedule lists under the 1950 Constitution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Residuary powers under the 1935 Act vested in the Governor-General, not the Federal Legislature. This contrasts sharply with the Indian Constitution, where residuary powers rest with Parliament.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Federal legislative supremacy over Concurrent subjects was enshrined in the 1935 Act, mirrored by Article 254 of the Constitution.

Value Addition:
• Canada's Constitution Act 1867 also vests residuary powers in the federal government — a comparison sometimes drawn in UPSC context.
• The Indian Constitution's choice to vest residuary powers in Parliament (Union) rather than an executive was a deliberate departure from the colonial model.
• The Concurrent List under the 1950 Constitution has 52 subjects (as amended), expanded from the 1935 Act's 36.

solution.concept_anchor: Provincial autonomy real but limited by Governor's reserve powers

statement_analysis.statement: Provincial autonomy introduced under the 1935 Act was absolute in nature, with Governors bound to act on ministerial advice in all matters.
statement_analysis.reason: Provincial autonomy was real but severely limited — Governors retained powers of 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' that allowed them to act without or against ministerial advice in specified matters.

statement_analysis.statement: The distinction between a Governor's 'constitutional discretion' and 'individual judgment' under the 1935 Act is that the former required no ministerial consultation while the latter required consultation but allowed override.
statement_analysis.reason: This is reversed. 'Individual judgment' required no ministerial advice at all, while 'special responsibilities' required consultation with ministers but permitted the Governor to override their advice — 'constitutional discretion' is a broader term.

statement_analysis.statement: Provincial Autonomy under the 1935 Act came into effect in 1937 when Congress and other parties formed ministries in several provinces following elections.
statement_analysis.reason: Provincial autonomy became operative on April 1, 1937, and the 1937 provincial elections led to Congress forming governments in six of eleven provinces.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (1 only) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is clearly incorrect, but students may assume only one statement is wrong and try to find the single incorrect one, missing that Statement 2 is also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1 — the claim of 'absolute' autonomy with Governors bound in 'all matters' is directly contradicted by the Governor's individual judgment and special responsibilities powers; Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Examine Statement 2 — the description reverses the actual legal meanings of 'individual judgment' (no consultation) and 'special responsibilities' (consultation but can override); Statement 2 is also NOT correct.
Examine Statement 3 — provincial autonomy did come into effect in 1937 with Congress-led ministries formed after elections; Statement 3 is correct.
Both Statements 1 and 2 are not correct, matching option b (1 and 2 only) as the answer to 'which are NOT correct.'
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension trap: students know provincial autonomy was introduced and may accept the word 'absolute' without scrutiny, forgetting that the Governors' overriding powers fundamentally compromised it. Statement 2 exploits reversed-causation by swapping the definitions of two closely related legal terms that most students recall in a generalized way without pinning down which required consultation and which did not.
solution.final_explanation:
Provincial Autonomy was the most significant operative feature of the 1935 Act, but its quality was vigorously contested even at the time — Congress leaders described Governors as operating parallel governments.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Autonomy was not absolute. Governors exercised 'individual judgment' (no ministerial advice needed) and 'special responsibilities' (consult but can override), severely curtailing ministerial authority.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The description reverses the legal categories. 'Individual judgment' permitted action without any ministerial advice; 'special responsibilities' required consultation but allowed the Governor to override ministers.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Provincial autonomy came into force on April 1, 1937, following elections in which Congress won majorities in six provinces.

Value Addition:
• Congress initially refused to form governments until assurances were obtained that Governors would not use their special powers arbitrarily — the 'office acceptance' controversy of 1937.
• Congress ministries resigned en masse in October–November 1939 after India was declared a belligerent in WWII without consultation.
• The Governor's role under Article 163 of the 1950 Constitution is far more circumscribed than under the 1935 Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Governor-General's reserved subjects — Defence, Foreign Affairs, Ecclesiastical

statement_analysis.statement: Prevention of grave menace to peace or tranquility was listed among the Governor's 'special responsibilities' under the 1935 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Governor's special responsibilities explicitly included prevention of grave menace to peace or tranquility, protection of minorities, and safeguarding of British commercial interests.

statement_analysis.statement: Defence and External Affairs were subjects over which the Governor-General exercised direct control, independent of the Federal Executive Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Defence, External Affairs, and Ecclesiastical Affairs were reserved subjects under the Governor-General's direct control and were not subject to the Federal Executive Council's advice.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 1935 Act, the Governor's 'individual judgment' powers and 'special responsibilities' powers are legally identical — both permit action without any ministerial advice.
statement_analysis.reason: These are distinct legal categories. 'Individual judgment' required no ministerial consultation at all, while 'special responsibilities' required the Governor to consult ministers but permitted override of their advice — a critical procedural difference.

statement_analysis.statement: Safeguarding of British commercial interests in India was explicitly listed as one of the Governor's special responsibilities under the 1935 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The protection of British commercial interests was indeed one of the enumerated special responsibilities of Governors, reflecting the colonial economic objectives embedded in the Act.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) would be chosen by students who conflate 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' as functionally the same, making Statement 3 appear correct and pushing the count to all four.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — prevention of grave menace to peace is a well-documented special responsibility of Governors; Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 2 — Defence, External Affairs, and Ecclesiastical affairs were Governor-General's reserved subjects not subject to Executive Council; Statement 2 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 3 carefully — 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' are distinct: the former needs no consultation, the latter requires consultation but allows override; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 4 — safeguarding British commercial interests is an enumerated special responsibility; Statement 4 is correct.

Three of the four statements are correct, so the answer is option b (Only two... wait — three correct = option c). Re-check: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct = three correct = option c. But option c = Only three. Correct answer is c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 3 is central to this question. Both 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' allowed the Governor to act contrary to ministerial wishes, and students with surface-level knowledge treat them as synonymous. The critical legal distinction — that special responsibilities required prior consultation while individual judgment bypassed consultation entirely — is what separates a precise answer from an approximate one.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act created a layered architecture of executive powers that is essential for UPSC analysis questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Prevention of grave menace to peace was an enumerated special responsibility, giving Governors broad powers to act independently.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Defence, External Affairs, and Ecclesiastical matters were reserved under the Governor-General and excluded from the Federal Executive Council's jurisdiction.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: 'Individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' are distinct. Individual judgment required no consultation; special responsibilities mandated consultation but allowed override.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Protection of British commercial interests was explicitly named as a Governor's special responsibility, revealing the colonial agenda embedded in the autonomy framework.

Three of four statements are correct → answer is option c.

Value Addition:
• The three categories of Governor's authority under the 1935 Act — constitutional functions, special responsibilities, individual judgment — had no parallel in any prior constitutional legislation.
• Governors' special responsibilities were a major reason Congress demanded assurances before forming ministries in 1937.
• Article 163 of the Indian Constitution restricts the Governor's discretion far more narrowly than the 1935 Act did.
solution.final_explanation_corrected: Correction note: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct = three correct statements. The answer is option c (Only three).

solution.concept_anchor: Federal Court jurisdiction types and Privy Council as final appellate body
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps the descriptions of original and advisory jurisdiction, exploiting the common confusion between who can approach the court (original = units/federation only; advisory = Governor-General's reference) — a subtle but critical distinction.
elimination_logic: Match A (Original Jurisdiction) — original jurisdiction of the Federal Court covered disputes between the federation and units or inter-unit disputes; only governmental entities could approach, not individuals; matches with 3.
Match B (Appellate Jurisdiction) — the Federal Court heard appeals from High Courts in British India on constitutional matters, but final appeals lay with the Privy Council in London; matches with 1.

Match C (Advisory Jurisdiction) — the Governor-General could refer questions of law to the Federal Court for an advisory opinion; this was discretionary and non-binding in some senses; matches with 4.
Match D (Final Appellate Authority) — the Privy Council in London, not the Federal Court, was the final appellate body — a key distinction from the Supreme Court of India; matches with 2.
The correct matching is A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2, which is option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The critical trap is associating the Federal Court with final appellate authority — the role actually held by the Privy Council in London. Students who know the Federal Court was the apex judicial body in India may assume it also served as the final court of appeal, conflating its structural position with its functional jurisdiction. Additionally, the distinction between original jurisdiction (open only to governmental units) and individual access is frequently missed.
solution.final_explanation:
The Federal Court, established in 1937, was India's first apex judicial institution — a significant constitutional innovation under the 1935 Act.

Correct Matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2

• A (Original Jurisdiction) → 3: Only the federation and its constituent units (provinces/states) could invoke original jurisdiction; individual citizens had no access.
• B (Appellate Jurisdiction) → 1: The Federal Court heard constitutional appeals from High Courts in British Indian provinces.
• C (Advisory Jurisdiction) → 4: The Governor-General could refer questions of constitutional law to the Federal Court for a non-binding opinion.
• D (Final Appellate Authority) → 2: The Privy Council in London remained the final court of appeal — the Federal Court was not sovereign in this sense.

The trap pairing is B and D — students often assign 'final appellate authority' to the Federal Court itself.

Value Addition:
• The Federal Court was established on October 1, 1937, and sat in Delhi.
• It was replaced by the Supreme Court of India on January 28, 1950.
• The Privy Council's continued supremacy was a major limitation on India's judicial sovereignty before 1950.
• Federal Court's first Chief Justice was Sir Maurice Gwyer.

concepts_used: Dyarchy: Abolition at Provinces, Introduction at Centre

solution.concept_anchor: Dyarchy reversed — abolished at provinces, introduced at Centre
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are correct, and students who do not scrutinize the causal link may assume R automatically explains A, missing that the abolition of provincial dyarchy and the introduction of central dyarchy are independent policy decisions with different rationales.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy at the provincial level (which was introduced by the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919) and simultaneously introduced dyarchy at the Centre for the first time.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Reserved subjects at the Centre included Defence, External Affairs, and Ecclesiastical Affairs — these were kept under the Governor-General's direct control.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The enumeration of reserved subjects at the Centre describes the content of central dyarchy, not the reason why provincial dyarchy was abolished. The abolition of provincial dyarchy was driven by the push for responsible government in provinces; the introduction of central dyarchy was driven by Britain's desire to retain imperial control at the Centre. These are independent policy choices, and R does not explain why A occurred.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT causally explain A — the answer is option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the reversed-causation trap. The Assertion and Reason are both factually accurate, and students reading quickly will accept option a. The critical insight is that the abolition of dyarchy in provinces and its introduction at the Centre were not causally linked — they were parallel but independent decisions. The reason merely describes what central dyarchy looked like (reserved subjects), not why provincial dyarchy was simultaneously abolished. The causal link students assume — 'dyarchy moved from provinces to Centre' as a single administrative transfer — is an oversimplification that does not hold legally.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act's treatment of dyarchy represents one of constitutional history's most instructive reversals. Dyarchy at the provincial level had been introduced by the Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) but was widely criticized as unworkable. The 1935 Act abolished it in provinces and granted full responsible government there. Simultaneously, it introduced dyarchy at the Centre for the first time, dividing federal subjects into Reserved (Defence, External Affairs, Ecclesiastical — under Governor-General) and Transferred (under Executive Council).

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The 1935 Act reversed the dyarchy arrangement — abolishing it at the provincial level and introducing it at the Centre.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Defence, External Affairs, and Ecclesiastical Affairs were indeed the central reserved subjects under the Governor-General's exclusive control.
• Causal Link — R does NOT explain A: R describes the content of central dyarchy, not the rationale for abolishing provincial dyarchy. These were independent political decisions.

Correct answer: option b.

Value Addition:
• Central dyarchy under the 1935 Act was never actually operationalized since the Federal Part never came into force.
• The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) introduced dyarchy at provinces in 1919 — often called the 'devolution rules'.
• Critics called provincial dyarchy a 'farce' because transferred subjects (health, education) had no real power or funds.

concepts_used: Simon Commission and Round Table Conferences as Precursors

solution.concept_anchor: Simon Commission to 1935 Act — legislative pathway sequence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a places the White Paper before the Joint Parliamentary Committee but after the Round Table Conferences, which sounds plausible since the White Paper was a government response to the conferences — students who know the individual steps but not the exact sequence fall into this trap.
elimination_logic: Anchor Point 1: The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927 and submitted its report in 1930 — this must come first in any sequence involving the 1935 Act's legislative history.

Anchor Point 2: The three Round Table Conferences (1930, 1931, 1932) followed the Simon Commission's appointment and were convened precisely because of the political controversy around the Simon Commission.
Anchor Point 3: The White Paper of 1933 was the British government's synthesis of Simon Commission report and Round Table Conference discussions — it preceded the Joint Parliamentary Committee.
Anchor Point 4: The Joint Parliamentary Committee examined the White Paper, and its report formed the basis of the Government of India Bill that became the 1935 Act.
The correct sequence is Simon Commission → Round Table Conferences → White Paper → JPC → Government of India Act 1935, which matches option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap targets candidates who know the individual steps but confuse the White Paper and the Joint Parliamentary Committee's relative order, or who place the Round Table Conferences before the Simon Commission report (since conferences began in 1930 and the report also came in 1930). The key is that Simon Commission submitted its report in May 1930, the first Round Table Conference was in November 1930, and the two processes were sequential, not parallel.
solution.final_explanation:
The legislative journey to the 1935 Act involved several distinct stages, each a response to the political controversies of the previous one.

Correct sequence: Simon Commission (1927–1930) → Round Table Conferences (1930–1932) → White Paper (1933) → Joint Parliamentary Committee (1933–1934) → Government of India Act 1935

• Simon Commission (1927–1930): Appointed to review the 1919 Act; boycotted by all Indian parties due to absence of Indian members. Its report provided the administrative blueprint.
• Round Table Conferences (1930–1932): Three conferences in London bridged Indian political opinion (Congress absent in 1st and 3rd, present in 2nd with Gandhi).
• White Paper (March 1933): The British government's formal proposals synthesizing earlier inputs.
• Joint Parliamentary Committee: Scrutinized the White Paper; its 1934 report formed the basis of the Government of India Bill.
• Government of India Act 1935: Passed in August 1935 — the longest act passed by the British Parliament at that time.

Value Addition:
• Congress boycotted the Simon Commission and the Joint Parliamentary Committee deliberations but participated in elections under the 1935 Act.
• The 1935 Act contained 321 sections and 10 schedules — the most elaborate constitutional legislation of the British Empire.
• Lord Linlithgow chaired the Joint Parliamentary Committee.

solution.concept_anchor: Scheduled Castes — reserved seats in joint electorates, not separate electorates
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (separate electorates) is a strong distractor because students know the 1935 Act extended separate electorates broadly and may assume Scheduled Castes received the same treatment as Muslims and Sikhs, not recalling the Poona Pact distinction.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a Scheduled Caste leader voting in 1937 provincial elections — identify the correct electoral arrangement for Scheduled Castes under the 1935 Act.

Eliminate option a (separate electorates for Scheduled Castes) — the Poona Pact (1932) specifically replaced Macdonald Award's separate electorates for Scheduled Castes with reserved seats in general (joint) electorates.
Eliminate option b (no representation at all) — Scheduled Castes had reserved seats in the general electorates after the Poona Pact, so they did have representation.
Eliminate option d (same electoral arrangement as Europeans) — Europeans had separate electorates; Scheduled Castes had reserved seats in joint electorates — entirely different arrangements.
Select option c — Scheduled Caste candidates stood in general (joint) electorates with reserved seats, and all voters in that constituency (including non-SC voters) voted for the SC reserved seat.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This scenario exploits the conflation between 'separate electorates' (as given to Muslims, Sikhs, Europeans, Anglo-Indians) and 'reserved seats in joint electorates' (as given to Scheduled Castes under the Poona Pact). Students who remember the 1935 Act broadly extended communal representation may assume Scheduled Castes received separate electorates. The Poona Pact (1932) was specifically designed to prevent this — Gandhi's fast-unto-death against the Communal Award forced Ambedkar to accept reserved seats rather than separate electorates.
solution.final_explanation:
The communal representation provisions of the 1935 Act must be understood in the context of the Communal Award (1932) and the Poona Pact that modified it.

The Communal Award (Macdonald Award) of 1932 originally proposed separate electorates for Scheduled Castes. Gandhi undertook a fast-unto-death against this, leading to the Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar. The Pact replaced separate electorates with reserved seats in general electorates — this arrangement was incorporated into the 1935 Act.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Scheduled Castes did not receive separate electorates under the 1935 Act. The Poona Pact replaced that proposal.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Scheduled Castes had reserved seats in joint electorates — they were represented.
• Option (c) — Correct: Scheduled Castes received reserved seats in general (joint) electorates, where all voters in the constituency participated in electing the reserved-seat candidate.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Europeans received separate electorates; this was a fundamentally different arrangement from reserved seats in joint electorates.

Value Addition:
• Communities with separate electorates under the 1935 Act: Muslims, Sikhs, Europeans, Anglo-Indians, Indian Christians.
• The Poona Pact increased the number of reserved seats for Scheduled Castes compared to what the Communal Award had proposed.
• Separate electorates were abolished by the Indian Constitution — Article 325 prohibits them.

solution.concept_anchor: Federal Legislature never came into existence — only Provincial operationalized
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Council of State) is a strong distractor because students know it was the proposed upper house and may assume it was part of a functioning legislature, not recalling that the entire Federal Legislature remained unimplemented.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: three of the four items either actually came into existence under the 1935 Act or were directly operationalized by 1937.
Provincial Legislature — came into existence in 1937 under the Provincial Part of the Act; it was operationalized.
Federal Court — established and became functional in October 1937 under the Act.
Reserve Bank of India — established in 1935 under provisions related to the Act.

Council of State (proposed Federal Upper House) — was NEVER constituted because the Federal Part of the Act was never implemented; it is the odd one out — the institution that was designed but never came into existence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap works here because the Council of State is a real institution named in the 1935 Act with detailed provisions (260 members, 6-year terms, etc.). Students who recall these specifics may treat it as an implemented institution, forgetting that the entire Federal Legislature — including both the Council of State and the Federal Assembly — was never constituted because the All-India Federation never materialized.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act created detailed blueprints for several institutions, but not all of them were actually established.

• Provincial Legislature — Operational from April 1, 1937, when the Provincial Part of the Act came into force.
• Federal Court — Established and functional from October 1, 1937, hearing original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction cases.
• Reserve Bank of India — Established in April 1935 under provisions linked to the Act's monetary framework.
• Council of State (proposed upper house of the Federal Legislature) — Never constituted. The All-India Federation never came into existence because the required number of princely states never executed Instruments of Accession. The Council of State, along with the Federal Assembly, remained entirely on paper.

The odd one out is option d — the Council of State.

Value Addition:
• The Council of State was to have 260 members; the Federal Assembly was to have 375 members.
• Since the Federal Legislature never materialized, the Central Legislature under the 1919 Act continued to function until 1947.
• The Central Legislature's Constituent Assembly role in 1946–1949 operated under an entirely different framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Instrument of Accession — 1935 Act precursor to post-1947 mechanism

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Government of India Act 1935, princely states were required to accede to the All-India Federation on a uniform basis with no scope for negotiating the terms of their accession.
statement_analysis.reason: Accession under the 1935 Act was voluntary and states could negotiate the terms, limiting accession to specific subjects — unlike British Indian provinces which had no such flexibility.

statement_analysis.statement: The Instrument of Accession mechanism used after 1947 to integrate princely states into the Indian Union was legally and conceptually derived from the accession framework introduced in the Government of India Act 1935.
statement_analysis.reason: The post-independence Instrument of Accession that Sardar Patel used to integrate princely states drew directly on the conceptual framework of the 1935 Act's voluntary accession mechanism, though the post-1947 context was fundamentally different.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is correct and students who do not scrutinize Statement 1 carefully may accept the broad claim about the accession framework being uniform, making both seem plausible.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — it claims accession was on a 'uniform basis with no scope for negotiation.' The 1935 Act explicitly allowed states to accede limited to specific subjects and to negotiate terms; this makes Statement 1 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the post-1947 Instrument of Accession is indeed recognized as conceptually derived from the 1935 Act's framework; Statement 2 is correct.
With Statement 1 incorrect and Statement 2 correct, the answer is option d (Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a partial-truth trap — it correctly identifies that princely states used an Instrument of Accession under the 1935 Act but incorrectly adds 'uniform basis with no scope for negotiation,' which directly inverts the actual provision. Students who know the accession mechanism existed may not catch the error about its flexibility.
solution.final_explanation:
The Instrument of Accession under the 1935 Act is a concept with long constitutional genealogy.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 1935 Act's accession mechanism was explicitly voluntary and negotiable. Unlike British Indian provinces that were automatically part of the federation's structure, princely states could negotiate the scope of their accession — limiting it to specific subjects. The claim of a 'uniform basis with no scope for negotiation' is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon's post-independence instrument of accession drew on the legal concept developed in the 1935 Act, though the political circumstances were entirely different — post-independence accession was driven by Partition and decolonization, not a negotiated British constitutional scheme.

Value Addition:
• The 1935 Act required 52 of 104 Chamber of Princes seats plus states with half the total princely population to accede before the federation could form — this threshold was never met.
• Post-1947, over 500 princely states signed Instruments of Accession within a few months — a political achievement of a very different order.
• Hyderabad and Junagadh's refusal to accede led to military action (Operation Polo) and police action respectively.

solution.concept_anchor: Council of India abolished by 1935 Act — Secretary of State continued
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know the 1935 Act made major changes to the India Office may assume the Secretary of State himself was abolished alongside the Council, not recognizing that the office of Secretary of State continued with modified powers.
elimination_logic: Identify what body was abolished by the 1935 Act at the India Office level — it was the Council of India, not the Secretary of State.
Eliminate option a (Board of Control) — the Board of Control was abolished by the Government of India Act 1858, not 1935.
Eliminate option c (Secretary of State for India) — the Secretary of State continued; only the advisory Council was abolished.
Eliminate option d (Viceroy's Executive Council) — this body was not abolished by the 1935 Act.
The correct answer is option b — the Council of India.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Council of India' with 'Secretary of State' — two closely linked but distinct bodies. Students who know the 1935 Act restructured the India Office may vaguely recall that 'something was abolished' and choose the more prominent entity (Secretary of State) rather than the advisory council that was actually abolished.
solution.final_explanation:
The administrative apparatus connecting London to India underwent significant changes through various constitutional acts.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Board of Control was a creation of Pitt's India Act 1784 and was abolished by the Government of India Act 1858, not 1935.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Council of India, established by the Government of India Act 1858 as an advisory body to the Secretary of State, was abolished by the 1935 Act. The Secretary of State could now act with greater independence, aided by a smaller group of advisors.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Secretary of State for India was not abolished — the office continued until Indian independence in 1947.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Viceroy's Executive Council was not abolished by the 1935 Act.

Value Addition:
• The Council of India had 15 members initially under the 1858 Act — it was a powerful check on the Secretary of State's authority.
• Its abolition was seen as a step toward reduced direct bureaucratic control from Whitehall over Indian affairs.
• The India Office itself was dissolved only in August 1947 when Indian independence was proclaimed.

solution.concept_anchor: RBI established 1935, nationalized 1949 — not established by RBI Act alone
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students know the RBI Act 1934 was the primary legislation for the bank's establishment, and may not recall that its establishment is also linked to the constitutional context of the 1935 Act; the pair appears contradictory.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option a — RBI established in 1935 and nationalized in 1949. RBI was established on April 1, 1935, originally as a private shareholders' bank, and was nationalized under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act 1948, effective January 1, 1949. This pair is correct.
Evaluate option b — RBI established in 1934 is incorrect; while the RBI Act was passed in 1934, the bank commenced operations on April 1, 1935.
Evaluate option c — RBI as a government department from inception is incorrect; it started as a private shareholders' bank.
Evaluate option d — nationalization in 1947 alongside independence is incorrect; nationalization happened in 1949.
Option a is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the common confusion between the RBI Act (1934) and the RBI's actual establishment date (April 1, 1935). Additionally, the nationalization date (1949, not 1947) is frequently confused with the independence year. Students who conflate legislative enactment with institutional establishment will select option b.
solution.final_explanation:
The Reserve Bank of India's history involves two important dates that are regularly tested.

• Option (a) — Correct: The RBI was established on April 1, 1935 (under the RBI Act 1934, with its establishment linked to the 1935 constitutional framework), originally as a private shareholders' bank. It was nationalized on January 1, 1949.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The RBI Act was passed in 1934, but the bank commenced operations on April 1, 1935 — not 1934.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The RBI was not a government department from inception; it was a private shareholders' bank with authorized capital held by private investors.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Nationalization occurred in 1949, not in 1947 at independence. The Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act was passed in 1948.

Value Addition:
• The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) first recommended an independent central bank for India.
• Sir Osborne Smith was the RBI's first Governor.
• The RBI was initially headquartered in Kolkata and moved to Mumbai (then Bombay) in 1937.

solution.concept_anchor: PSCs made statutory — first time — under 1935 Act

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1935 made the establishment of Public Service Commissions a statutory requirement for the first time, transforming them from ad hoc advisory bodies into legally mandated institutions.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act established the Federal Public Service Commission and mandated Provincial Public Service Commissions by statute for the first time, serving as the direct precursor to Articles 315–323 of the Indian Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 1935 Act, two or more provinces could establish a Joint Public Service Commission to serve their shared needs, subject to the approval of the Federal Legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act did permit Joint Public Service Commissions for two or more provinces, but the approval mechanism was not specified as Federal Legislature approval — it was a separate statutory provision; the characterization of the approval requirement here is a fabrication.

statement_analysis.statement: The Federal Public Service Commission established under the 1935 Act was a direct institutional precursor to the Union Public Service Commission created under the Indian Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The FPSC under the 1935 Act evolved directly into the UPSC under the 1950 Constitution, with Articles 315–323 codifying and expanding the statutory framework first introduced in 1935.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is the strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are both accurate and the error in Statement 2 (the Federal Legislature approval requirement) sounds institutionally plausible.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — PSCs becoming statutory for the first time under the 1935 Act is a well-established fact; Statement 1 is correct.

Scrutinize Statement 2 — Joint PSCs were permitted but the specific approval requirement attributed to the Federal Legislature is not an established provision; this addition makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — the FPSC → UPSC institutional lineage is unambiguous; Statement 3 is correct.
With Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect, the answer is option b (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the scope-extension trap by adding a plausible but incorrect administrative detail — Federal Legislature approval — to an otherwise accurate statement about Joint PSCs. Students who know Joint PSCs were permitted under the 1935 Act may accept the entire statement without examining the approval mechanism claim.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act's contribution to civil services administration was foundational, embedding the principle of statutory, independent service commissions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before 1935, Public Service Commissions existed but were not legally mandated. The 1935 Act made them statutory for the first time — a significant transformation in the institutional basis of merit-based recruitment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While Joint PSCs for two or more provinces were indeed permitted, the statement's addition of a Federal Legislature approval requirement is inaccurate and unsupported by the Act's provisions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Federal Public Service Commission under the 1935 Act was the direct precursor to the UPSC, with the constitutional framework in Articles 315–323 building on and expanding the 1935 statutory model.

Value Addition:
• The 1919 Act had created a Public Service Commission but without the same statutory mandate.
• Articles 315–323 of the Indian Constitution deal with establishment, composition, and functions of UPSC and State PSCs.
• The UPSC's independence from executive interference was a conscious extension of the 1935 Act's statutory basis.

solution.concept_anchor: 1935 Act expanded franchise to ~14%, not universal suffrage

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1935 introduced universal adult franchise for the first time in India, extending voting rights to all adults regardless of property or educational qualifications.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act only expanded the franchise to approximately 35 million people (about 14% of the population) on the basis of property, tax payment, and literacy qualifications — universal adult franchise was introduced only by Article 326 of the 1950 Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: Women's franchise was extended under the 1935 Act on the same qualifying terms as men — a notable expansion though still based on property and literacy criteria.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act included women voters on the same qualifying basis as men — property, tax, or educational qualifications — representing a significant though still limited step toward gender equality in electoral participation.

statement_analysis.statement: The electorate under the 1935 Act remained smaller than under the Government of India Act 1919, as more restrictive qualifying criteria were introduced to prevent mass political participation.
statement_analysis.reason: The electorate significantly expanded from approximately 7 million under the 1919 Act to approximately 35 million under the 1935 Act — the 1935 Act expanded, not contracted, the franchise.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (1 only) is a strong distractor because Statement 1's false claim about universal suffrage is the most obvious error, and students may stop after identifying it, missing that Statement 3 is also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — universal adult franchise was not introduced by the 1935 Act; only ~14% of the population received voting rights; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — women's franchise on the same terms as men under the 1935 Act is accurate; Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — the electorate expanded from 7 million to 35 million; the claim that it became smaller is directly false; Statement 3 is also NOT correct.
Both Statements 1 and 3 are not correct, matching option c (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension trap — adding 'universal' and 'regardless of property or educational qualifications' to an otherwise partial truth (franchise was expanded). Statement 3 reverses a quantitative fact (expansion presented as contraction). Students who read Statement 3 quickly may miss the inversion because the general direction of their knowledge ('the 1935 Act was restrictive') matches the distorted claim.
solution.final_explanation:
The franchise provisions of the 1935 Act represent both progress and continued colonial limitation.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Universal adult franchise was not introduced in 1935. The franchise was expanded to approximately 35 million (about 14% of India's population) on the basis of property, tax payment, or educational qualifications. Universal adult franchise came with Article 326 of the 1950 Constitution.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Women were included in the expanded electorate on the same qualifying terms as men — property, literacy, or tax criteria. This was a meaningful though limited step.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: This is a factual reversal. The electorate grew from approximately 7 million under the 1919 Act to approximately 35 million under the 1935 Act — a fivefold expansion.

Value Addition:
• Universal adult suffrage (Article 326) gave voting rights to all citizens 21 years and above; later reduced to 18 by the 61st Constitutional Amendment (1988).
• The 1935 Act's expanded electorate participated in the landmark 1937 provincial elections — India's first mass democratic exercise under limited franchise.
• The expansion from 3% (1919) to 14% (1935) represented the most significant pre-independence franchise extension.

solution.concept_anchor: Congress won majority in 6 of 11 provinces in 1937 elections

statement_analysis.statement: Jawaharlal Nehru described the Government of India Act 1935 as 'a machine with strong brakes but no engine.'
statement_analysis.reason: Nehru's famous characterization of the 1935 Act as 'a machine with strong brakes but no engine' captured Congress's critique that the Act provided elaborate machinery for control but no real power for Indian self-governance.

statement_analysis.statement: Congress won clear majorities in eight of the eleven provinces in the 1937 provincial elections held under the Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Congress won outright majorities in six of eleven provinces (Madras, Central Provinces, Bihar, Orissa, United Provinces, Bombay), not eight. It formed coalition governments in some others.

statement_analysis.statement: Congress ministries collectively resigned from all provinces in 1939 following India's unilateral declaration as a participant in the Second World War without consulting Indian political leadership.
statement_analysis.reason: The Viceroy Lord Linlithgow's declaration of India as a belligerent in WWII in September 1939 without consulting Congress led to the mass resignation of all Congress provincial ministries between October and November 1939.

statement_analysis.statement: Congress boycotted both the deliberations of the Joint Parliamentary Committee and the subsequent 1937 provincial elections to maintain consistency in its rejection of the Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Congress boycotted the Joint Parliamentary Committee deliberations but chose to contest the 1937 elections despite its formal rejection of the Act — this apparent contradiction was a deliberate strategic decision to use the political space the elections provided.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two) is the strong distractor because students might identify Statement 2 as wrong (confusing 6 vs 8 provinces) but accept Statement 4 without checking whether Congress actually boycotted the elections, making them count only one incorrect statement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Nehru's 'machine with strong brakes' quote is well-documented; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Congress won majorities in 6 provinces, not 8; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — mass resignation of Congress ministries in 1939 following WWII declaration is historically accurate; Statement 3 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Congress boycotted JPC deliberations but did contest the 1937 elections, making the second claim in Statement 4 false; Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct, so the answer is option a (Only two correct).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a partial-truth trap — Congress did win an impressive number of provinces but the number is 6, not 8. Statement 4 uses conflation — Congress did boycott the JPC (true) and the student may extend this boycott posture to the elections (false) based on Congress's overall opposition to the Act. The apparent contradiction (rejecting the Act but contesting elections) is itself a historically important point that UPSC tests.
solution.final_explanation:
Congress's relationship with the 1935 Act was defined by strategic pragmatism overlaid with ideological opposition.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nehru's characterization was apt — the Act created elaborate institutional machinery but concentrated real power with the Governor-General and Governors.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Congress won majorities in 6 (not 8) of 11 provinces: Madras, Central Provinces, Bihar, Orissa, United Provinces, and Bombay. It formed governments in some others through coalitions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: All Congress provincial ministries resigned between October–November 1939 after Lord Linlithgow declared India a belligerent in WWII without consulting Indian leaders.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Congress boycotted JPC deliberations but actively contested the 1937 elections — a deliberate strategic decision to use provincial autonomy as a political platform while rejecting the Act's overall framework.

Two correct = option a.

Value Addition:
• Muhammad Ali Jinnah described the 1939 resignation day as 'Deliverance Day' — a sign of deteriorating Congress-Muslim League relations.
• Congress's 1937 election success and subsequent ministry experience strengthened the independence movement significantly.
• The six provinces where Congress won majorities represented a majority of India's population.

concepts_used: Relationship between the 1935 Act and the Indian Constitution of 1950

solution.concept_anchor: Features NOT borrowed from 1935 Act — Fundamental Rights, DPSP, Preamble

statement_analysis.statement: The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and States through three lists in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution was modelled on the three-list structure of the Government of India Act 1935.
statement_analysis.reason: The Seventh Schedule's Federal, State, and Concurrent Lists drew directly from the 1935 Act's tripartite distribution, which was acknowledged by the Constituent Assembly debates.

statement_analysis.statement: The Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Part III of the Indian Constitution were adapted from the rights framework embedded in the Government of India Act 1935.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act contained no fundamental rights provisions whatsoever. Part III of the Indian Constitution was an original addition inspired by the United States Bill of Rights and other sources — not derived from the 1935 Act.

statement_analysis.statement: Emergency provisions enabling the Centre to assume control over states, reflected in Articles 352, 356, and 360 of the Indian Constitution, drew from the emergency and Governor-General powers framework of the 1935 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act's provisions for the Governor-General to suspend provincial autonomy and assume direct control served as the template for the emergency provisions in the Constitution, though the 1950 Constitution required parliamentary sanction — a key democratic modification.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is the correct answer, but option b (2 and 3 only) is a strong distractor for students who incorrectly recall that the 1935 Act had some rights provisions.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — the Seventh Schedule's three-list structure is well-established as derived from the 1935 Act; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the 1935 Act had absolutely no fundamental rights provisions; this is a definitive fact; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — the emergency provisions in Articles 352, 356, and 360 are recognized as drawing from the 1935 Act's emergency framework; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — the answer is option c (1 and 3 only). [Note: option d in the question is 1, 2 and 3 — check answer]
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the critical trap — students who know the 1950 Constitution borrowed heavily from the 1935 Act may reason that since the Constitution has extensive rights, some rights framework must have existed in the 1935 Act too. This is false. The complete absence of fundamental rights in the 1935 Act — and the fact that Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, and the Preamble were all original constitutional additions — is the most important distinction between the two documents.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between the 1935 Act and the 1950 Constitution is one of the most frequently tested themes in UPSC constitutional history questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Seventh Schedule's tripartite list structure (Union List, State List, Concurrent List) was directly modelled on the 1935 Act's Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent Lists — the most direct legislative borrowing.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 1935 Act had no fundamental rights provisions. Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12–35) was an entirely original contribution, drawing from the US Bill of Rights, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and other sources.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Articles 352, 356, and 360 of the Indian Constitution (National Emergency, President's Rule, Financial Emergency) drew from the 1935 Act's framework, with the critical democratic modification of requiring parliamentary approval.

Correct answer: option c (1 and 3 only).

Value Addition:
• Other features borrowed from the 1935 Act: Federal Court → Supreme Court; FPSC → UPSC; Governor's institution; bicameral legislature concept.
• Features entirely absent from 1935 Act: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Preamble, universal suffrage, sovereign democratic republic character.
• Ambedkar acknowledged structural borrowings but emphasized the 1950 Constitution's fundamentally democratic spirit.

concepts_used: Emergency Powers and Central Control over Provinces

solution.concept_anchor: 1935 emergency powers — unilateral executive acts vs. parliamentary sanction under 1950 Constitution
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Governor-General could suspend provincial autonomy and assume direct control under the 1935 Act, and this served as the template for Article 356 (President's Rule) in the Indian Constitution.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. R claims the 1935 Act required parliamentary approval before the Governor-General could exercise emergency powers. This is false — the 1935 Act's emergency provisions were unilateral executive acts that did not require legislative sanction, unlike Article 356 of the Indian Constitution which requires parliamentary approval.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect — even without evaluating causal relationship — the answer must be option c (A correct, R incorrect).
The final step identifies option c as the correct answer — consistent with correct_option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in R adds 'parliamentary approval' to the 1935 Act's emergency powers — a democratic safeguard that was absent in 1935 but present in the 1950 Constitution. Students who know both documents may inadvertently apply the 1950 Constitution's procedural safeguard to the 1935 Act's executive-dominated provision. This reversal is precisely what UPSC tests — the critical difference between the two emergency frameworks is not their structure but their democratic accountability.
solution.final_explanation:
Emergency powers are among the most significant and controversial provisions in both the 1935 Act and the Indian Constitution.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The Governor-General's power to suspend provincial autonomy and assume direct control under the 1935 Act was the direct historical precursor to Article 356 (President's Rule). This genealogy is well-acknowledged in constitutional scholarship.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The 1935 Act's emergency provisions did NOT require parliamentary approval. They were unilateral executive acts — the Governor-General could act on Crown authority without legislative sanction. This contrasts sharply with Article 356 of the Indian Constitution, which requires Parliament to approve the proclamation within two months and thereafter every six months.

The critical democratic distinction: The 1950 Constitution added parliamentary oversight to emergency powers — a fundamental departure from the colonial model of executive unilateralism embedded in the 1935 Act.

Correct answer: option c.

Value Addition:
• The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) added further safeguards to Article 352 requiring cabinet recommendation in writing.
• The S.R. Bommai case (1994) significantly curtailed the misuse of Article 356.
• Under the 1935 Act, the Governor also had powers to dissolve provincial assemblies and impose Governor's Rule within provinces — a parallel to the Governor-General's central emergency powers.

statement_analysis.reason: Burma's separation was effected through the Government of Burma Act 1935 — a separate but simultaneous piece of legislation — not as a provision within the Government of India Act 1935 itself.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Burma and Aden were separated from British India in 1937, as part of the broader administrative reorganization accompanying the 1935 constitutional reforms.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Burma (effective April 1, 1937) and Aden (also 1937) were separated from British India as part of the wider reorganization accompanying the 1935 Act, though each was governed by separate legislation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is correct and Statement 1's error (conflating the Government of Burma Act with a provision of the Government of India Act) is a subtle legislative distinction that most students don't scrutinize.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 carefully — Burma's separation was through the Government of Burma Act 1935, which was companion but separate legislation from the Government of India Act 1935; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — both Burma and Aden were separated in 1937 as part of the broader reorganization; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — the answer is option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two distinct pieces of legislation — the Government of India Act 1935 and the Government of Burma Act 1935 — treating them as one document. Since both were enacted in the same year and are functionally related, students commonly attribute Burma's separation to a provision 'within' the 1935 Act rather than recognizing it as a separate legislative instrument. UPSC frequently tests this kind of precision about legislative identity.
solution.final_explanation:
The separation of Burma from British India is a significant event in colonial administrative history, often misattributed legislatively.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Burma was separated not by a provision within the Government of India Act 1935, but through the Government of Burma Act 1935 — a separate legislative instrument enacted alongside but distinct from the India Act. The separation became effective on April 1, 1937.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Both Burma and Aden were separated from British India in 1937 as part of the broader administrative reorganization that accompanied the 1935 constitutional reforms. Burma had been part of British India since 1886 following the Third Anglo-Burmese War.

Value Addition:
• Burma's separation in 1937 was preceded by years of debate about whether Burma should remain part of India — the Rangoon Separation Conference (1931) was a key step.
• Aden became a Crown Colony upon separation from India in 1937, later becoming part of South Yemen.
• Myanmar (formerly Burma) gained full independence in 1948, separate from India's 1947 independence.

solution.concept_anchor: Orissa carved from Bihar and Orissa Province — linguistic basis
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students know Sindh was carved from Bombay Presidency and may confuse Orissa's parent province (Bihar and Orissa) with Bengal, which is a geographically adjacent and historically relevant province.
elimination_logic: Identify the correct parent province for Orissa — the province was 'Bihar and Orissa' (a combined province), from which Orissa was carved out; not Bengal.
Eliminate option b — Orissa was not carved from Bengal Presidency; it came from the Bihar and Orissa Province.
Eliminate option c — NWFP was elevated from a Chief Commissioner's Province to a Governor's Province, not created afresh from Punjab; it was not 'carved from Punjab' in the same sense.
Eliminate option d — the reorganization of 1935 was on administrative and communal lines, not linguistic lines; the linguistic reorganization came with the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
Option a correctly states that Sindh was separated from Bombay Presidency and Orissa from the Bihar and Orissa Province.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap places Bengal as Orissa's parent province — a plausible error since Bengal is adjacent to Orissa and students may confuse the 'Bihar and Orissa Province' (a distinct administrative unit created in 1912) with Bengal. The key is recalling that Bihar and Orissa were already combined as a province since 1912, and it was this combined province that was split to create Orissa in 1936.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1935 Act's administrative reorganization created new provinces, reshaping British India's map.

• Option (a) — Correct: Sindh was separated from Bombay Presidency and Orissa was carved from the Bihar and Orissa Province (effective 1936). Orissa's separation was partly on linguistic grounds — Odia-speaking identity.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Orissa was not carved from Bengal; it came from the Bihar and Orissa Province, which had been a combined administrative unit since 1912.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The North-West Frontier Province was elevated from a Chief Commissioner's Province to a full Governor's Province — it was not newly carved from Punjab in 1935, though it had been separated from Punjab earlier.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 1935 Act's provincial reorganization was driven by administrative, communal, and political considerations — not the linguistic principle that governed the States Reorganisation Act 1956.

Value Addition:
• The Bihar and Orissa Province was created in 1912 by separating Bengal Presidency.
• The demand for a separate Orissa Province based on Odia linguistic identity had been active since the late 19th century.
• The 1956 States Reorganisation Act created state boundaries along linguistic lines — a fundamentally different basis from the 1935 provincial reorganization.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparing residuary powers placement — 1935 Act vs. Indian Constitution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a swaps the residuary powers entries between the two documents, exploiting the most common error: attributing Parliament as the residuary authority under the 1935 Act (which is actually the 1950 Constitution's position).
elimination_logic: Match A (Residuary powers under 1935 Act) — the 1935 Act vested residuary powers in the Governor-General, not the Federal Legislature; matches with 2.
Match B (Residuary powers under Indian Constitution 1950) — Article 248 and Entry 97 of Union List vest residuary powers in Parliament; matches with 4.
Match C (Federal List subject count under 1935 Act) — the Federal List had 59 subjects; matches with 1.
Match D (Concurrent List subject count under 1935 Act) — the Concurrent List had 36 subjects; matches with 3.
Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3, which is option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap swaps the residuary powers entries: students who know residuary powers go to Parliament under the Indian Constitution may apply this to the 1935 Act as well, selecting option a. The correct answer requires knowing the 1935 Act placed residuary powers with the Governor-General — an executive, not a legislature — which is the defining contrast between the two constitutional frameworks.
solution.final_explanation:
The distribution of powers under the 1935 Act and the Indian Constitution share structural similarities but have critical differences.

Correct Matching: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3

• A (Residuary powers under 1935 Act) → 2 (Governor-General): Residuary legislative authority under the 1935 Act was vested in the Governor-General, not any legislative body — colonial control demanded this executive concentration.
• B (Residuary powers under Indian Constitution) → 4 (Parliament/Union): Under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List, Parliament has exclusive power over residuary subjects — a democratically accountable legislature, not an executive.
• C (Federal List subject count, 1935 Act) → 1 (59 subjects): The Federal List had 59 subjects.
• D (Concurrent List subject count, 1935 Act) → 3 (36 subjects): The Concurrent List had 36 subjects under the 1935 Act.

Value Addition:
• Provincial List under the 1935 Act had 54 subjects.
• The Indian Constitution's Union List has 100 items, State List 61, and Concurrent List 52 (as currently amended).
• Canada's Constitution vests residuary powers federally — influencing both the 1935 Act and the Indian Constitution's approach to the Union.

solution.concept_anchor: Governor-General's certification power — bills rejected by legislature
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because 'reserve powers' sounds like the correct constitutional category for the Governor-General's authority to act unilaterally, and students may not distinguish between the broader category (reserve powers) and the specific mechanism (certification) that applied to rejected bills.
elimination_logic: Identify what specific power allowed the Governor-General to bring a bill into effect despite the Federal Legislature's refusal to pass it — this was the certification power.
Eliminate option a (proclamation power) — proclamation power related to emergency, not to certifying rejected bills.
Eliminate option b (reserve powers) — reserve powers is a broader category; the specific mechanism for overriding legislative rejection was certification, not a general reserve power invocation.
Eliminate option c (ordinance-making power) — ordinances were issued when the legislature was not in session, not when it rejected a bill.
Select option d (certification power) — the Governor-General could certify a bill as essential for safety or tranquility even if the legislature had rejected it, bringing it into effect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap offers 'reserve powers' as option b — a real constitutional term that sounds like it should encompass the Governor-General's authority over rejected bills. Students with broad knowledge may select this without recognizing that the 1935 Act had a distinct and specific mechanism — the certification power — for this precise situation, separate from the general category of reserve powers.
solution.final_explanation:
The Governor-General's authority over legislation under the 1935 Act was extraordinary by any constitutional standard.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Proclamation power related to emergency declarations, not to overriding legislative rejection of specific bills.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While 'reserve powers' is a real constitutional category, the specific mechanism for certifying rejected bills was the 'certification power' — a distinct and precisely defined authority.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ordinance-making power was exercised when the Federal Legislature was not in session — not as a response to legislative rejection of a bill.
• Option (d) — Correct: The certification power allowed the Governor-General to certify a bill as essential for the safety or tranquility of British India, bringing it into effect despite the legislature's refusal to pass it.

Value Addition:
• The Governor-General could also issue 'Governor-General's Acts' on his own initiative when the legislature was not in session.
• These extraordinary powers meant the Federal Legislature under the 1935 Act was fundamentally subordinate to the executive — unlike Parliament's sovereignty under the 1950 Constitution.
• The Governor-General's certification power had no parallel in the Indian Constitution's relationship between President and Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: Federal Court ≠ Supreme Court — Privy Council remained final appellate body
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Federal Court as the final court of appeal) is the strongest distractor because students know the Federal Court was the highest judicial body in India and assume this made it the final court of appeal, not recognizing that the Privy Council retained that role.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option a — Federal Court as the final court of appeal in India: incorrect, the Privy Council in London remained the final court of appeal above the Federal Court.
Evaluate option b — Federal Court established in 1937 with original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction: both the year and the three-fold jurisdiction description are accurate.
Evaluate option c — Federal Court replaced by Supreme Court in 1947: incorrect, the replacement happened on January 28, 1950, not at independence in 1947.
Evaluate option d — Original jurisdiction was accessible to individual citizens: incorrect, original jurisdiction was available only to the federation and its units, not individuals.
Option b is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits the entity-swap trap — swapping 'Privy Council' (the actual final appellate body) with 'Federal Court' (the apex court within India). Students who recall that the Federal Court was India's highest court may automatically conclude it was also the final court of appeal, missing the critical jurisdictional limitation that required appeals beyond the Federal Court to go to London.
solution.final_explanation:
The Federal Court's jurisdiction and limitations are among the most precisely tested aspects of the 1935 Act.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Federal Court was NOT the final court of appeal. Appeals from the Federal Court lay with the Privy Council in London — a fundamental limitation on India's judicial sovereignty.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Federal Court was established in 1937 and exercised original jurisdiction (inter-governmental disputes), appellate jurisdiction (constitutional appeals from High Courts), and advisory jurisdiction (Governor-General's references).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Federal Court was replaced by the Supreme Court of India on January 28, 1950 (when the Constitution came into force), not in 1947 at independence.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Original jurisdiction of the Federal Court was NOT available to individual citizens — only the federation and its constituent units (provinces/states) could invoke it.

Value Addition:
• The Federal Court operated from 1937 to 1950 — 13 years.
• Its first Chief Justice was Sir Maurice Gwyer; its last was Sir Harilal Kania, who became the first Chief Justice of India.
• The Privy Council's role as final appellate body was abolished only when the Indian Constitution came into force in 1950.

Provincial Autonomy: Nature, Scope, and Limitations

solution.concept_anchor: Dyarchy abolished at provinces — full responsible government introduced 1937
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly states that dyarchy was abolished but incorrectly suggests that the Governor lost all special powers, which would make provincial autonomy genuinely absolute — a misreading that sounds like the natural consequence of abolishing dyarchy.
elimination_logic: Identify the constitutional principle: the 1937 scenario involves a minister asking why certain decisions go to the Governor rather than the cabinet — this tests understanding of what dyarchy's abolition actually meant.
Eliminate option a — if dyarchy persisted, there would be reserved and transferred subjects, but dyarchy was specifically abolished at the provincial level by the 1935 Act.

Eliminate option b — dyarchy was indeed abolished, but the Governor retained individual judgment and special responsibility powers even after abolition; the claim of no special powers is an overextension.
Eliminate option d — the federal structure's non-implementation only affected the Centre, not provincial governance.

Select option c — dyarchy was abolished, giving ministers full responsible government over the transferred sphere, but Governors retained 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibility' powers that continued to limit ministerial authority in specific areas.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b's scope-extension trap adds 'with no special powers remaining' to the accurate fact that dyarchy was abolished — making it sound like a complete ministerial victory. Students who know dyarchy was abolished may not remember that the Governor's individual judgment and special responsibility powers survived abolition and continued to restrict ministerial authority, making provincial autonomy 'real but limited.'
solution.final_explanation:
The 1937 scenario captures the precise constitutional ambiguity that Congress leaders experienced in the provincial ministries they formed after the elections.

Dyarchy at the provincial level (introduced in 1919) divided subjects into Reserved (under Governor) and Transferred (under ministers). The 1935 Act abolished this division — all subjects theoretically fell under ministerial responsibility. However, the Governor's 'individual judgment' and 'special responsibilities' powers survived the abolition of dyarchy and created a different but equally effective limitation on ministerial authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Dyarchy was abolished by the 1935 Act at the provincial level; no reserved/transferred distinction existed from 1937.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While dyarchy was abolished, Governors retained individual judgment and special responsibility powers — the claim of 'no special powers' is factually wrong.
• Option (c) — Correct: Dyarchy was abolished, but Governor's individual judgment (no consultation needed) and special responsibilities (consultation required but can override) powers continued, creating a qualified rather than absolute ministerial authority.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The non-implementation of the Federal Part affected central governance, not provincial arrangements, which were fully operationalized.

Value Addition:
• Congress demanded Governor's assurances before forming ministries in 1937 precisely because of these surviving powers.
• The 'office acceptance controversy' of 1937 revolved around whether Governors would use special powers to interfere with Congress ministries.
• Governor's Rule at the provincial level was a further mechanism by which the Centre could override provincial autonomy.
